'''LAC Minerals''' was a Canadian [[mining]] company established in 1981 with extensive mineral holdings in [[North America]] and [[South America]]. They specialized in mining [[Precious metal|precious metals]], but also had [[copper]] and [[Zinc mining|lead-zinc mines]]. In 1994 they were purchased by [[Barrick Gold|Barrick Gold Corporation]].<ref name="Farnsworth">{{cite news|last = Farnsworth | first = Clyde H. | title = Lac Minerals Agrees to Friendly Takeover |  newspaper = The New York Times | date = 25 August 1994 | url = https://www.nytimes.com/1994/08/25/business/company-news-lac-minerals-agrees-to-friendly-takeover.html?pagewanted=1 | accessdate =16 September 2009}}</ref>

==Corporate history==
Originally incorporated in [[Quebec]] in 1981 as Long Lac Minerals Ltd., the company's name was changed to LAC Minerals Ltd. the following year when it acquired Les Terrains Aurifères Malartic (Québec) Ltée, Les Mines-Est Malartic Ltée, and Willroy Mines Ltd.  In 1985, LAC Minerals Ltd. acquired Lake Shore Mines Limited, Little Long Lac Gold Mines Limited, and Wright-Hargreaves Mines Limited.  In 1992, the company changed its name to '''Lac Minerals Ltd.'''.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Company Detail: LAC Minerals Ltd.|publisher=Canadian Corporate Reports, McGill Digital Archives|url=http://digital.library.mcgill.ca/hrcorpreports/search/detail.php?company=LAC%20Minerals%20Ltd.&ID=1003}}</ref> In 1994, [[Royal Oak Mines]] attempted a [[Takeover#Hostile takeovers|hostile takeover]] of the company,<ref>{{Cite news|author=Staff|date=26 July 1994|title=A Big New Bidder for Lac Minerals|newspaper=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/07/26/business/company-news-a-big-new-bidder-for-lac-minerals.html}}</ref> but a more attractive bid was made by Barrick Gold, and Lac Minerals was acquired by AB Acquisition Inc., which was a wholly owned subsidiary of American Barrick Resources Corporation, since 1995 known as Barrick Gold Corporation.<ref name="Farnsworth" />

===International Corona lawsuit===
{{main|Lac Minerals Ltd. v. International Corona Resources Ltd.}}
In 1983 International Corona, a smaller mining corporation, sued LAC Minerals for breach of fiduciary duty after LAC had purchased a mining property out from under Corona, when Corona had done all of the exploratory work and had shared the information with LAC.  The result in [[Lac Minerals Ltd. v. International Corona Resources Ltd.]] was a clear statement by the [[Supreme Court of Canada]] on the nature of fiduciary and confidential relationships that can be created in the course of business, together with appropriate remedies for restitution when such relationships are breached.<ref>{{Cite web|title = Confidential Information and Joint Ventures |author1=Leitl, Steven H.  |author2=Perry, Chrysten E.|url = http://www.macleoddixon.com/documents/Confidential_Information_and_JVs.pdf |publisher = Macleod Dixon|accessdate = 2011-12-20}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Protection of Trade Secrets and Confidential Information|author = Edward Fan|url = http://www.torys.com/Publications/Documents/Publication%20PDFs/AR2008-39.pdf|publisher = [[Torys LLP]]|accessdate = 2011-12-20|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120407012510/http://www.torys.com/Publications/Documents/Publication%20PDFs/AR2008-39.pdf|archive-date = 2012-04-07|url-status = dead}}</ref> The stock price of LAC Minerals dropped considerably on the Toronto Exchange upon the [[Ontario Supreme Court]]'s ruling in March 1986.<ref>{{Cite news|author=Staff|title=Lac Minerals Shares Tumble After Court Order To Give Up Rich Gold Claim|newspaper=Ottawa Citizen|date=11 March 1986|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=2194&dat=19860311&id=VK8yAAAAIBAJ&sjid=qu8FAAAAIBAJ&pg=1171,389574}}</ref>

===Friends of Santa Fe County lawsuit===
In 1990 the Friends of Santa Fe County sued LAC Minerals over a number of environmental issues based on LAC Minerals' exploratory work and initial mining in the gold fields of the [[Ortiz Mountains]].  Some of the claims were dismissed,<ref>''Friends of Santa Fe County v. Lac Minerals'', 892 F. Supp. 1333 (D.N.M. 1995)</ref> but an eventual settlement was reached. Under the settlement, LAC Minerals was required to clean up a plume of groundwater contaminated by nitrates and cyanide that had resulted from the [[heap leaching]] of gold ore. Also under the settlement, 1,350 acres of the mine were donated to the Santa Fe Botanical Garden for the [[Ortiz Mountain Educational Preserve]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Ortiz Mountains gold mine reclamation|publisher=New Mexico Environmental Law Center|url=http://nmenvirolaw.org/index.php/site/cases/ortiz_mountains_gold_mine_reclamation/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20091004033651/http://nmenvirolaw.org/index.php/site/cases/ortiz_mountains_gold_mine_reclamation/|archivedate=4 October 2009|url-status=live}}</ref>
